newsitem.title: USA: Arafat worried about Mideast peace process.
newsitem.headline: Arafat worried about Mideast peace process.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said on Wednesday he was worried about the future of the Mideast peace process because of Israel's decision last week to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem.
"I am worried. Truly, I am worried," Arafat said in a speech at Rice University here. He described the building of 6,500 new Jewish homes, as "very dangerous."
"No one can accept this," he said.

The Palestinians see Arab East Jerusalem, which the Israelis captured in the 1967 Middle East war, as the capital of a future Palestinian state while Israel says Jerusalem will always be its undivided capital.

Jerusalem's fate was to be discussed in upcoming talks between the Palestinians and Israelis. Arabs fear that Israel is staking a claim to the disputed territory by putting up the housing, although Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his intent was to ease a housing crisis for both Jews and Arabs.

Arafat said it was imperative that the United States jump in to help resolve the crisis. He said President Bill Clinton, who earlier this week criticised the Israeli move, had promised in talks at the White House to do what he could.
"I am trusting him," Arafat said of Clinton's pledge. "He promised to save the peace process."

Arafat said, despite the problems, his commitment to the peace process was strong, fuelled in part by memories of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was gunned down in November 1995 by a Jewish extremist opposed to his pursuit of peace with the Palestinians.
"I can't forget that the peace which we had achieved is an open target. I cannot forget that my partner Rabin had lost his life for this peace," he said.
"For this ... we are completely committed to the peace process," Arafat said. "There is no turning back, no other alternative but to continue."

Arafat was in Houston to visit former President George Bush and former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, both of whom he praised for having played a key role in bringing Arabs and Israelis to the bargaining table after many years of acrimony.
Earlier in the day, he briefed the United Nations Security Council on the Jewish settlements issue, then flew to Georgia to visit former President Jimmy Carter.
After conferring privately with members of the Security Council, Arafat said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "pushing the peace process in very critical and crucial circumstances."
